content.title: Paraphrased Contamination Evades N-gram Overlap But Not Perplexity Gap: Results on Five Benchmarks
content.text:
We built a contamination detector for language-model benchmarks and ran it on five internal benchmarks against a 7B model trained on a 3.1 trillion token corpus we index in full. Its two components catch largely disjoint things, and the disjointness is the result.

The first component is 13-gram overlap. For each benchmark item, we take the question and the reference answer, tokenize with the model's tokenizer, and look up every 13-gram in a suffix-array index over the pretraining corpus. An item is flagged if more than 30 percent of its 13-grams occur at least once. We chose 13 because it sits above the length at which generic phrasing ("which of the following statements") collides by chance in a 3T corpus; at 8-grams the chance-collision rate on freshly written control items was 22 percent, at 13 it was 0.6 percent.

The second component is a perplexity gap. For each item we generate eight paraphrases with a separate model, filter them with a human pass that rejected 11 percent for changing the meaning, and compute the 7B model's per-token log-likelihood on the original and on each paraphrase. The gap is the original's mean log-likelihood minus the mean over paraphrases. A model that has memorized the exact wording assigns it a higher likelihood than it assigns semantically equivalent rewordings; a model that merely knows the subject should be roughly indifferent. We flag items whose gap exceeds a per-benchmark threshold set so that 5 percent of freshly written control items in the same format are flagged.

Here are the flag rates. QuarryQA (factual short answer, 4,000 items): n-gram 11.2 percent, perplexity gap 12.8 percent, overlap between the two sets 9.1 percent. LedgerMath (word problems, 2,500 items): n-gram 3.4 percent, perplexity gap 17.9 percent, overlap 3.3 percent. Sable-Code (function completion, 1,800 items): n-gram 27.0 percent, perplexity gap 21.4 percent, overlap 19.6 percent. Tidewater-NLI (entailment pairs, 5,000 items): n-gram 0.8 percent, perplexity gap 4.9 percent, overlap 0.5 percent. Orrery-Reasoning (multi-step logic, 1,200 items): n-gram 2.1 percent, perplexity gap 6.2 percent, overlap 1.9 percent.

LedgerMath is the anomaly. Almost everything n-gram found, perplexity gap also found, but perplexity gap found 14.6 percent of items that n-gram missed entirely. We pulled 200 of those items and searched the corpus for their numeric answers together with any two content nouns from the problem. In 163 of them we located a near-duplicate problem in a widely redistributed instruction-tuning dataset: same structure, same numbers, but with the character names changed, the objects changed (apples to notebooks), and sentence order shuffled. No 13-gram survives that treatment. The model's likelihood on the original wording was nonetheless elevated, because what it memorized was the structure and the number sequence, and the original is closer to that template than any paraphrase is.

To check this was not a story we were telling ourselves, we ran a controlled experiment. We took a sixth benchmark that had been held out of all training, paraphrased 500 of its items with the same name-and-object substitution recipe, and continued pretraining a 1.3B model on a 20B token mixture with those paraphrases inserted an average of 3.2 times each. We then ran both detectors on the original items. At a 5 percent false-positive rate on controls, 13-gram overlap recalled 4.0 percent of the contaminated items (it caught the ones where the recipe left a long numeric expression intact). Perplexity gap recalled 71.2 percent. Including verbatim rather than paraphrased contamination, n-gram recall rose to 96 percent and perplexity gap to 88 percent, so the two are complementary rather than one dominating.

The perplexity-gap detector has a false-positive mode that we did not anticipate. Items written to a rigid template, such as multiple-choice stems that all begin identically, show a positive gap even when uncontaminated, because paraphrasing breaks the template and the model has seen the template form millions of times in unrelated data. On Tidewater-NLI, whose items are highly formulaic, our initial false-positive rate on controls was 9.3 percent instead of the intended 5. The fix was to compute the gap relative to a baseline: we generate synthetic items in the same template with fabricated content, measure their gap, and subtract its mean. That brought the control false-positive rate to 3.1 percent and reduced the Tidewater flag rate from 7.7 to 4.9 percent. A second false-positive source is numbers: paraphrases sometimes re-tokenize a number differently (1,200 versus 1200), which shifts likelihood for reasons unrelated to memorization. We now normalize number formatting before paraphrasing.

Does this matter for scores? Removing perplexity-gap-flagged items from LedgerMath dropped the 7B model from 61.2 to 54.8 percent; removing only n-gram-flagged items dropped it to 60.1. The 6.4 point drop is the honest number; 1.1 is what n-gram-only decontamination would report.

Limitations. The perplexity-gap method requires token-level log-likelihoods, which rules out most API-only models. It cannot distinguish contamination from legitimate exposure: a model that studied the same textbook a benchmark author drew from will show an elevated gap on those problems, and we do not think that is cheating, but the detector does. Thresholds are calibrated per benchmark and per model and do not transfer. Paraphrase quality is a dependency we have not fully characterized; a paraphraser that shares training data with the model under test could produce paraphrases the model finds unusually likely, shrinking the gap. And memorization at frontier scale may differ in ways a 1.3B controlled experiment does not capture.

notes: Original research write-up with two detectors, per-benchmark numbers, a controlled contamination experiment, a false-positive analysis with a concrete mitigation, and honest limitations. A correct judge should notice the surprising result (paraphrased contamination: 4 percent n-gram recall vs 71 percent perplexity-gap recall) and the FPR mechanism (formulaic templates inflate the gap).
